extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers and prose stylists (especially thriller and general fiction authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for creative writers about how long sentences should be and when to use short vs. long sentences; covers tone, voice-consistency, emotional use-cases, musicality, and editing. Focused on sentence-level craft within fiction prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence length: short vs. long
rubrics_metrics.description: Short sentences are more dramatic; long sentences are calmer by nature and tend to be more explanatory or descriptive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thriller writers favor short sentences; many genres (except some literary prose) lean toward leaner sentences as attention spans constrict. Use short sentences for drama and pace; use long sentences for calmer, explanatory, or descriptive passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with the narrative voice
rubrics_metrics.description: The way to do that is to make sure the sentence is consistent with the narrative voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A long or ornate sentence must fit the established voice of the narration; mismatch will yank the reader out of the story. If your overall style is lean and ‘mean,’ long sentences should be used sparingly and only when they align with voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long sentences should exult in expansiveness while moving to their close
rubrics_metrics.description: A long sentence should exult in its own expansiveness, lovingly extending its line of thought while being always clearly moving to its close. It should create anticipation, not confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing long sentences, keep clear forward motion toward a close so the reader feels guided. The hard part is telling the difference between expansive anticipation and confusing meandering; ensure syntactic and semantic direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writer must remain in control (avoid reader confusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A long sentence can seem thrillingly out of breath, deliciously tantalizing, so long as we feel the writer is still in charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the reader has to stop and figure out what you meant, the sentence has failed. Maintain control through clarity of thought and structure; avoid overloading reader short-term memory by delaying the full stop unnecessarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid showy virtuosity that bedazzles the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: A long sentence should give pleasure without provisos, not buttonhole and bedazzle the reader with virtuosity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t write sentences that exist to showcase syntactic dexterity at the expense of reader engagement. Anti-pattern: sentences that make readers think, 'Who does this joker think he is? Just get on with it!'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prose is the servant of the story
rubrics_metrics.description: The prose is the servant of the story, not the other way around.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stylistic choices—including sentence length and ornament—should always prioritize serving the story. If style highlights itself over plot, character, or emotion, it’s counterproductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use long sentences to show inner life and emotional intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: Long sentences can be used to show us the inner life of a character in moments of high emotional intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In moments of heightened feeling, a sustained sentence rhythm can mirror agitation or flood of thought. Example: Horace McCoy’s passage that gives the impression of someone walking fast and agitated. Use long sentences selectively for interiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long sentences can perform multiple functions (triple duty)
rubrics_metrics.description: A long sentence can provide a window into the narrator’s inner life, weave in description of place, and include a bit of exposition — triple duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-crafted long sentences can combine interiority, description, and exposition economically. Ensure each function is integrated smoothly so the sentence still moves to a satisfying close.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar and clarity remain essential in long sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: It should not just be about ensuring that the sentence is grammatically correct, or even clear. The one true aim ... was 'to enhance life—to give the self (the soul) body by wedding it to the world.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond ambition to 'enhance life,' long sentences still require grammatical correctness and clarity; do not overburden the reader’s short-term memory. Technical control (correct punctuation, parallel structure, clear clauses) supports ambitious sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate musicality/unobtrusive poetry in sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: A great long sentence should be a look at life with more 'alertness'... Every writer is a poet by default and every sentence a little poem. The longer the sentence, the more closely it resembles poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for 'a bit of magic' or 'unobtrusive poetry'—phrases that 'sing'—but keep the poetry unobtrusive so it enhances rather than distracts. Musicality should serve meaning and emotion, not stylistic showmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be willing to try and delete if it fails
rubrics_metrics.description: So don’t be afraid to expand the occasional sentence if the moment is right. If it doesn’t work out, you can hit the delete key.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment with longer sentences when appropriate; ruthless editing is part of craft. If the sentence doesn’t serve the story or reader, remove it.
